finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id deletes the report without enforcing authorization. authorize() is called without await, so its 403 rejection never stops the handler, and db.reports.remove runs regardless of the user's grants.
finding.source: Any request to DELETE /reports/:id. The only precondition is that the request reaches this route. Nothing in this file requires a logged-in user, and req.user may be undefined (line 5).
finding.sink: db.reports.remove(report.id) at server.js:21 (destructive write on a protected resource)

trace.note: DELETE route handler registered; attacker controls req.params.id
db.reports.get(req.params.id) loads the report; no check that it exists
authorize(req.user, 'delete', report) is called without await. It returns a pending promise and the handler continues synchronously
Inside authorize: db.grants lookup is async; if user is undefined, user.id throws and becomes a rejected promise
403 is thrown only in the rejected promise, which nothing awaits or catches
remove executes and the report is deleted before or regardless of the rejection

finding.guards_checked: authorize() (lines 9-16) does perform the grant check, but the await is missing at line 20, so its throw is never observed. No try/catch, no route-level auth middleware, and no per-route authorization in this file. The session middleware that populates req.session is not in this file, so upstream auth could not be verified; if none exists, the bypass is unauthenticated.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check is authorize() (server.js:9-16), but its throw at line 14 becomes a rejected promise because line 20 calls it without await. The handler then reaches db.reports.remove at line 21 regardless. No try/catch, no route-level auth middleware, and no per-route check exist in this file. The session middleware that sets req.session (server.js:5) is not in this file, so an upstream login requirement could not be verified.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: server.js:20 calls authorize() without await, so its 403 rejection (server.js:14) is never observed and server.js:21 deletes the report whether or not the user holds a 'delete' grant. The attacker is any caller whose request reaches the route, which is a low-privilege or unauthenticated user rather than one who already holds delete power, and no effective control sits between them and the remove call. The one caveat is that line 5 throws if no session middleware exists upstream, which would make the route unreachable, but that is a missing dependency, not a control that blocks an attacker.

finding.claim: A single unauthorized PUT or DELETE can crash the Node process. The 403 thrown by authorize() in an async Express handler is never caught, which produces an unhandled promise rejection. On Node 15+ the default behavior is to terminate the process.
finding.source: Any request to PUT /reports/:id (line 25) or DELETE /reports/:id (line 18) for a report the caller lacks the action on, or for a nonexistent id, or with an unauthenticated session.
finding.sink: Process availability: unhandled rejection from authorize() at server.js:27 (PUT) and server.js:20 (DELETE, also via the null-report TypeError at server.js:21)

trace.note: await authorize(req.user,'write',report) on an unauthorized report: authorize throws 403 at line 14
The async handler rejects; Express 4 does not catch async handler rejections, so there is no error response and the request hangs
On DELETE, the un-awaited authorize rejects with no handler at all, which is unhandled
If db.reports.get returns null, authorize (line 10) and report.id (line 21) throw TypeError, also unhandled

finding.guards_checked: No try/catch, no Express error handler, no process.on('unhandledRejection') in this file. Severity depends on the Express version (Express 5 forwards async rejections to the error handler) and the Node version, neither of which is pinned here (no package.json in the directory).

verdict.guard_found: None in server.js: no try/catch, no Express error middleware, no process.on('unhandledRejection'). authorize() (server.js:9-16) throws and nothing catches it. Line 20 calls authorize without await, so its rejection is unhandled. The rest of the directory is empty apart from server.js; there is no package.json, so the Express and Node versions are unknown.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code (throw at server.js:14, awaited at server.js:27, un-awaited at server.js:20, null-report TypeError at server.js:10 and server.js:21), and an anonymous or low-privilege caller can reach it, but whether the process crashes depends on the Express version: Express 4 leaves the async rejection unhandled (crash on Node 15+), while Express 5 forwards it to the error handler and returns a 403. Since no package.json pins either version, the crash claim cannot be decided from this directory. A separate, version-independent problem is that server.js:20 does not await authorize(), so server.js:21 runs db.reports.remove() before the 403 is raised, meaning an unauthorized DELETE still deletes the report.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id is vulnerable to mass assignment. The entire req.body is passed to db.reports.update with no field allowlist, so a caller with write permission on a report can change any column, including ownership or identifier fields.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled JSON body in PUT /reports/:id (line 3 express.json parses it into req.body)
finding.sink: db.reports.update(report.id, req.body) at server.js:28 (write to all persisted report fields)

trace.note: express.json() parses the request body without a field filter
authorize(req.user,'write',report) passes for a caller with the write grant
req.body is forwarded unchanged to db.reports.update; keys such as owner_id, id, or permission fields are not filtered

finding.guards_checked: The write-grant check at line 27 is awaited and correct, so it stops callers without write permission. It does not limit which fields a permitted caller may write. The db layer is not in the repo, so whether it whitelists columns is unknown. Impact depends on the schema, which is also not present.

verdict.guard_found: server.js:27 `await authorize(req.user, "write", report)` is awaited and authorize throws a 403 at server.js:14-15 when the write grant is missing, so only callers with write on the report reach the update. No field allowlist exists in server.js; the update at server.js:28 forwards req.body unchanged. The db layer (db.reports.update, db.grants) is not in the repo, so any column whitelisting there is unknown.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code (express.json at server.js:3, handler at :25, awaited write check at :27, unfiltered req.body at :28), and the attacker is an authenticated user holding write on the report (server.js:9-16, :27). Whether that lets them change owner or identifier columns depends on the schema and on db.reports.update, neither of which is in the repo, so the impact cannot be decided. Separately, server.js:20 calls authorize without await in the DELETE handler, so the remove at :21 runs without waiting for the grant check; that is a stronger authorization bug than this finding and was outside the scope of this verification.
